stem: A 52-year-old man, retired after a long career as a warehouse supervisor, presents with about ten weeks of progressive mid-back pain that he initially attributed to years of heavy lifting on the job. Over-the-counter analgesics have given only partial relief, and over the past two weeks he has noticed mild difficulty with balance that his family has also remarked on. He denies fevers he's noticed but admits he hasn't checked his temperature and has lost some weight without trying. No prior TB treatment, no known TB contact, no known drug-resistant contact. MRI of the spine shows destruction of two adjacent vertebral bodies with a paraspinal collection, concerning for spinal TB (Pott's disease). CT-guided aspiration of the paraspinal collection was sent for molecular testing, which was positive for M. tuberculosis. Exam: point tenderness over the mid-thoracic spine, mild gait unsteadiness, no focal motor deficits, no fever.

patient.social_history: Lives with family; longstanding history of heavy manual lifting attributed as the cause of his back pain
patient.presenting_complaint: Progressive mid-back pain, new mild gait unsteadiness, unintentional weight loss
patient.exam_findings: Point tenderness over mid-thoracic spine, mild gait unsteadiness, no focal motor deficits, vertebral body destruction with paraspinal collection on imaging
patient.prior_treatment: Over-the-counter analgesics with only partial relief; no prior TB treatment

distractors: Mechanical back pain from a longstanding occupational lifting history proposed as sufficient explanation without imaging follow-through
Age-related degenerative spinal disease proposed as an alternative to an infectious or destructive process
Gait unsteadiness attributed to a benign balance issue of aging rather than a new neurological or structural concern
ntep_correct_actions: Perform upfront molecular testing (NAAT) directly on the accessible extrapulmonary specimen (the CT-guided paraspinal aspirate) as the first-line microbiological tool, rather than anchoring the workup around culture and histology as the primary reference standard.
who_correct_actions: Perform upfront molecular testing (NAAT) directly on the accessible extrapulmonary specimen (the CT-guided paraspinal aspirate) as the first-line microbiological tool, rather than anchoring the workup around culture and histology as the primary reference standard.
us_correct_actions: Anchor the diagnostic workup for this extrapulmonary presentation around culture and histology as the reference standard, treating molecular testing as a general, conditional adjunct rather than the upfront first-line tool for extrapulmonary specimens.
critical_error_conditions: Attributing the vertebral destruction and paraspinal collection entirely to a degenerative or mechanical process and deferring targeted aspirate sampling and molecular testing
expected_divergence_points: Whether upfront molecular testing on the accessible extrapulmonary specimen is the first-line diagnostic tool or culture/histology remains the anchoring reference standard
